doc.title: Hal Galper interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 27, 2022

title: Melody first, good note theory, Schillinger and Bob Sher's reharmonization class
summary: He writes melody first, uses good note theory, and credits Schillinger and Bob Sher's course on reharmonizing songbook tunes from ukulele changes with shaping his outlook.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: When you’re working on a composition over a length of time can I envision sheets of score paper with lines written out in chord symbols or is that not the way you work?

Melody first. I used to write harmony first but the melodies just came out very stilted. You have to do melody first. Once you’ve got the melody then I use something called good note theory, you know, which is: is this note going to be a natural 9 or a flat 9 or is it going to be a fifth of a chord. You know. So I will try it as different functions of different chords to see which sound I was looking for. Look I studied Schillinger so I have an analytical mind. You know. I took Schillinger for two years, that left me with the — thankfully with the tools. Because I couldn’t hear everything but I could figure it out

you know, because I had Schillinger. And that was a major, the two most important classes were that class and Bob Sher’s re-harmonization class which was re-harmonizing the American songbook from the ukulele changes into jazz changes. Fabulous course. I took to that like a duck to water. My nickname in Boston eventually was the “change master.” Because I could put changes to anything.
You just said a word that I didn’t get. The something changes instead of the jazz changes. Talking about the Broadway tunes.
Oh they were ukulele or guitar changes.

He had the early fake books which were the pictures of the Library of Congress cards. And that’s what we were working — this is pre Real Book, right? Where you had to buy the books surreptitiously, it was illegal to sell the book. You had to go to the black market to get the book you know. So and everybody is afraid they’re going to get arrested because they’re buying this book illegally. It’s hilarious. But and that was an amazing class, Bob Sher, who is also from my hometown, would sit at the piano and show you how to reharmonize these guitar symbols into chords and sing along these inane melodies with the changes you know. We used to call it Bob Sher’s cocktail hour because he’d sing along with the re-harms, you know?

Show how they work. Most valuable. That one and Schillinger. And it wasn’t ‘til many years later I realized how much Schillinger had affected my outlook, my general outlook on things. That there were reasons why things sounded good and reasons why they didn’t. And that’s what I wanted to find out: why things sounded good.
How much weight, when you’re re-harmonizing tunes, do the melody notes or note have in your choice of a chord to put with it?
Oh I just mentioned it. I can consider a note any function of a chord.

If I wanted to I could harmonize a melody all with sharp 9s on a dominant chord. Constant harmony it’s called. Or I could make them all sharp 11s. Or I could make them all thirds or fifths or ninths. That’s good note theory. Does this note sound good as a nine or a sharp nine or a sharp eleven, you play it over and over and over until the vibe gets to you and tells you what is the choice. The choices are all intuitive. This is not frontal lobe. You’ve just got to bang away at it until the message bubbles up from way down deep below in your early brain that this is the one that works you know.
